explanations.explanation: That's exactly what He says: "Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted." I think this one lands softly on a lot of hearts. Notice He doesn't say the mourning isn't real. He says comfort is coming for those who mourn.

Jesus actually makes the opposite promise. He says, "Blessed are those who mourn, for they will be comforted." I think that's a gentle one to read slowly. Comfort is what He promises to those who mourn.

explanations.answer: Who is blessed and what they'll get
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The poor in spirit get the kingdom of heaven, and those who mourn will be comforted. Each line names a group and then gives them a promise. It works like a label on a cookie box: who it's for, then what's inside.

explanations.answer: What to do and what to avoid
explanations.explanation: Close, but there are no instructions in these two lines. Jesus doesn't say "do this" or "don't do that." He names who is blessed, then says what they will get: the kingdom of heaven for the poor in spirit, comfort for those who mourn. Same shape both times.

explanations.answer: A question and then its answer
explanations.explanation: No questions here, friend. Jesus makes plain statements, one right after the other. First comes who is blessed, then what they'll receive: "theirs is the kingdom of heaven" and "they will be comforted." Same pattern, twice in a row.

That's it: "Blessed are those who hunger and thirst for righteousness, for they will be filled." Jesus promises a full plate to people who are starving for what's right. Nobody walks away from that table empty. I wish every batch I pulled out of the oven came with a promise like that.
Good guess, since life does test us. But Jesus' word here is not tested. He says those who hunger and thirst for righteousness "will be filled." The promise is fullness, plain and simple.

I get why humbled came to mind, because I've been humbled by a lopsided batch more than once. But that isn't what Jesus says in this line. He says those who hunger and thirst for righteousness "will be filled." That's the promise.
Jesus does promise them something. He says, "Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy." The line comes with a promise attached, same as the others. Mercy given gets mercy shown.

Right, there's a promise attached. Jesus says, "Blessed are the merciful, for they will be shown mercy." Every one of these blessings comes with something in return. This one is mercy for the merciful.
That's the word: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God." Jesus is talking about the heart, not the outside. And the promise is about as big as promises get: they will see God.
Proud is the word I'd pick after one good batch, so I can't blame you. But Jesus says the pure in heart are blessed, and they will see God (Matthew 5:8). He doesn't use proud anywhere in that line.
Bold sounds like a great heart to have, doesn't it? But Jesus' word is pure. "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God." That's the one He picked.
Yes, baker! "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God." That's a big name to be handed. Jesus gives it to the people who make peace.
Scribes were the men who copied and taught the Law, but they don't show up in these verses. The group Jesus names is the peacemakers. He says, "they will be called sons of God."
Shepherds, the folks who tend sheep, don't appear anywhere in these verses. Jesus says the peacemakers are blessed, for "they will be called sons of God." That's the group He names.
That's it. "Blessed are those who are persecuted because of righteousness." Jesus says they're persecuted for doing right, not for doing wrong. And He still calls them blessed.
I see why that came to mind, but Jesus says something different. He says they're persecuted because of righteousness. Those who suffer for doing right are the ones He calls blessed.

Foolishness is a fun guess, since I've been picked on for plenty of silly stamps myself. But Jesus' word is righteousness. "Blessed are those who are persecuted because of righteousness." He's talking about suffering for doing right.

Sharp eye, baker. To the poor in spirit, Jesus says, "theirs is the kingdom of heaven." To those persecuted because of righteousness, He says the very same words (Matthew 5:10). He starts and ends this stretch with the same promise.

Look at the two promises side by side. For the poor in spirit, it's "theirs is the kingdom of heaven." For those persecuted because of righteousness, it's "theirs is the kingdom of heaven" again (Matthew 5:10). It's the same promise, one at each end.

That's the instruction: "Rejoice and be glad." Jesus tells them to be glad even while they're being insulted and persecuted because of Him. And He gives them something to hold onto: "great is your reward in heaven."
That one makes sense, because being insulted hurts. But Jesus tells them something else: "Rejoice and be glad." He's speaking to people who are persecuted because of Him, and that's His word to them.
Running for cover is the first thing I'd do too, friend. But Jesus doesn't say that here. He says, "Rejoice and be glad." That's His word to those who are insulted and persecuted because of Him.
Yes! "Rejoice and be glad, because great is your reward in heaven." The reward is great, and it's waiting in heaven. Jesus gives them that to rejoice about.
It's an understandable guess, since the land matters a lot in the Old Testament. But in this verse Jesus puts their reward in heaven. "Great is your reward in heaven." That's where it is.
The temple was a big deal to the people listening, so I see the thinking. But Jesus doesn't mention it here. He says, "great is your reward in heaven."
Right. Jesus says, "for in the same way they persecuted the prophets before you." So if His listeners are persecuted, they're in good company. The prophets went through the same thing before them.

Jesus actually says the opposite. In verse 12 He says, "for in the same way they persecuted the prophets before you." The prophets were persecuted in the same way. His listeners would be following in their footsteps.

That's what He says: salt that loses its savor is "no longer good for anything, except to be thrown out and trampled by men." Jesus asks how it could be made salty again. He gives no answer, just where it ends up.
Nice idea, but Jesus doesn't mention it. He asks, "how can it be made salty again?" and then says it is "no longer good for anything, except to be thrown out and trampled by men."

explanations.answer: It's dried out in the sun
explanations.explanation: Sun-drying sounds like a thing a person would try, but it isn't in this verse. Jesus says the salt that loses its savor is "no longer good for anything, except to be thrown out and trampled by men."

Jesus says the opposite: "A city on a hill cannot be hidden." There's no "if it tries hard enough" in there. I'd try hiding on a hill in a tall white hat on a gold base, and I'd lose that game in about two seconds.
Right, there are no loopholes here. Jesus says, "A city on a hill cannot be hidden." It sits up high and everybody can see it. Trying harder doesn't change that.
That's where it goes. People "set it on a stand, and it gives light to everyone in the house." A lit lamp gets put up where it can do its job.
Under a bed is a creative hiding spot, I'll give you that. But Jesus says people don't hide a lit lamp. Instead, "they set it on a stand, and it gives light to everyone in the house."
A lamp in a closed-off room would only help whoever's in there. Jesus says they set it on a stand instead, "and it gives light to everyone in the house." The whole house gets the light.
Yes, baker. Jesus says, "let your light shine before men, that they may see your good deeds." He's talking about what they do. Good deeds are what people get to see.
I'd love for people to notice my apron, I'll admit it. But Jesus' word is deeds. "…that they may see your good deeds and glorify your Father in heaven."
A good fortune would be nice, friend, and my whole fortune was once a quarter. But Jesus says people will see their good deeds. That's the word in verse 16.
That's right. People see the good deeds and "glorify your Father in heaven." The glory goes up to Him. That's where Jesus points this whole thing.
The prophets did come up a few verses back, in verse 12, so I see the connection. But in verse 16, Jesus says people will "glorify your Father in heaven." That's who gets the glory.
Kings are the kind of folks who usually get the glory, so good thinking. But Jesus says people will "glorify your Father in heaven." He doesn't mention kings anywhere in this verse.
